newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Claims, factory orders.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Claims, factory orders.

text.p: If the U.S. credit markets move at all between now and Friday's jobs report, they will take baby steps, analysts said on Wednesday.

Data on weekly jobless claims and August factory orders should nudge prices somewhat higher, but with Treasury yields at the low end of a months-long trading range, most investors will wait for the big guns on Friday, the analysts said.
On Thursday, the sometimes-neglected jobless claims report will top the day's releases, some said.
"You could see a backup in prices if claims comes in around 350 (thousand)," said Carey Leahey, senior vice president and a senior economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc.
Economists in a Reuters survey on Friday projected initial claims held just about steady at 341,000 in the week ended September 28.

Last Thursday, a surprising boost in the number of initial claims helped buoy the bond market after the U.S. Labor Department said 340,000 people filed for unemployment benefits in the week ended September 21 against 329,000 the prior week.

"Claims have been bouncing around, but we had an important increase last week," said Peter Kretzmer, senior economist at NationsBanc Capital Markets Inc. "The market will be looking (at) whether that represents weakening in the labor market."
Kretzmer said Hurricane Fran, which slammed the North Carolina coast early last month, could have created work and temporarily suppressed jobless claims.

"I do think the labor market has weakened somewhat," he added. Later on Thursday morning, a report on August factory orders slated for 1000 EDT/1400 GMT will have little impact on the credit markets, the analysts said.
Last week's durable goods data already foreshadowed a marked decline in factory orders, they said. Durables orders slipped 3.1 percent in August, the largest decline since April 1995.
"Factory orders are fairly predictable, given that durables are about half of it and they've come in fairly strongly negative," Kretzmer said.
Although the factory orders report comprises non-durable items, economists do not expect strong gains in that sector.

"While non-durables were a surprise last month, most people are expecting the (factory orders) number to be down at least 1.5 percent," said Leahey. "We have a decline of 1.7 percent and I think the Street's right at the same spot."
In addition to interpreting economic data, the markets will hear comments from two Federal Reserve officials.

Fed Board Governor Edward Kelley is scheduled to speak at a Bank Holding Co Association seminar in Bloominton, Minnesota at 1400 EDT/1800 GMT, while Richmond Fed President Alfred Broaddus is booked for the Investors Roundtable in Wilmington, North Carolina at 1300 EDT/1700 GMT.
Neither will offer firm comments on inflation or monetary policy, fixed-income analysts said.
"I think they'll be very careful," said Astrid Adolfson, senior economist at MCM MoneyWatch Inc. "Everybody...has been told to speak...statesman-like."
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond should hew to its long-running trading range on Thursday, with a yield holding above 6.75 percent, analysts said.
